Monte Carlo sampling from a projected entangled-pair state
in simulations of quantum annealing in the three dimensional random Ising model

Jacek Dziarmaga Affiliation:  Jagiellonian University, Faculty of Physics, Astronomy and Applied Computer Science, Institute of Theoretical Physics, ul. Łojasiewicza 11, 30-348 Kraków, Poland Affiliation:  Jagiellonian University, Mark Kac Center for Complex Systems Research, ul. Łojasiewicza 11, 30-348 Kraków, Poland
June 1, 2026
Abstract

Quantum annealing with the D-Wave Advantage system in the random Ising model on a cubic lattice is simulated using a three-dimensional (3D) tensor network. The Hamiltonian is driven across a quantum phase transition from a paramagnetic phase to a spin-glass phase. The network is represented as a tensor product state, also known-particularly in two dimensions-as a projected entangled-pair state (PEPS). The annealing procedure is repeated for a range of annealing times in order to test the Kibble-Zurek (KZ) power law governing the residual energy at the end of the annealing ramp. For an infinite lattice with periodic nearest-neighbor random Ising couplings, the final energy is evaluated using a deterministic method. For a finite lattice with open boundaries, we introduce a more efficient Monte Carlo sampling approach. In both cases, the residual energy as a function of annealing time approaches the KZ power law as the annealing time increases.

I Introduction

The Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM), originally proposed to describe the formation of topological defects during cosmological phase transitions [67, *K-b, *K-c], was later adapted to continuous phase transitions in condensed matter systems. In this context, it evolved into a dynamical theory predicting how the density of defects scales with the quench rate according to the universality class of the transition [154, *Z-b, *Z-c, 35]. These predictions have been confirmed in numerous numerical studies [74, 146, 40, 3, 9, 153, 132, 133, 134, 144, 33, 129, 18, 77, 130] and experiments [21, 13, 110, 6, 15, 86, 81, 113, 142, 85, 54, 19, 84, 135, 101, 16, 76, 56, 75, 38, 37, 20, 147, 89, 78, 111]. The quantum version of the mechanism (QKZM) describes quenches across quantum critical points in isolated systems [32, 155, 98, 45, 46, 97, 119, 114, 87, 28, 22, 96, 122, 121, 42, 31, 34, 99, 30, 152, 123, 39, 61, 10, 36, 100, 125, 104, 82, 11, 112, 106, 107, 58, 12, 109, 112, 116, 91, 44, 43, 8, 55]. Its predictions have also been tested experimentally [113, 2, 7, 23, 17, 14, 52, 83, 66, 5, 143, 68, 120, 115].

The basic idea of QKZM can be summarized as follows (see also Refs. 46, 97, 35, 108 for reviews). A smooth ramp crossing the critical point at time tct_{c} can be linearized near the transition as

ϵ⁡(t)=t−tcτQ.\epsilon(t)=\frac{t-t_{c}}{\tau_{Q}}. (1)

Here ϵ\epsilon is a dimensionless parameter in the Hamiltonian that measures the distance from the quantum critical point, and τQ\tau_{Q} is the KZ quench time. Initially, the system is prepared in its ground state and follows the instantaneous ground state adiabatically far from the transition. Adiabaticity breaks down near the time t−tc=−t^t-t_{c}=-\hat{t}, when the energy gap becomes comparable to the quench rate,

Δ∝|ϵ|z​ν∝|ϵ˙/ϵ|=1/|t−tc|.\Delta\propto|\epsilon|^{z\nu}\propto|\dot{\epsilon}/\epsilon|=1/|t-t_{c}|. (2)

This condition defines the characteristic timescale t^∝τQz​ν/(1+z​ν),\hat{t}\propto\tau_{Q}^{z\nu/(1+z\nu)}, where zz and ν\nu are the dynamical and correlation-length critical exponents, respectively. The corresponding KZ correlation length,

ξ^∝t^1/z∝τQν/(1+z​ν),\hat{\xi}\propto\hat{t}^{1/z}\propto\tau_{Q}^{\nu/(1+z\nu)}, (3)

defines the characteristic length scale of KZ excitations after crossing the critical point.

Recent progress in programmable quantum simulators has opened new opportunities for exploring QKZM in higher dimensions. In particular, Rydberg-atom arrays enable versatile emulation of quantum many-body systems [49, 117, 120, 115], while coherent D-Wave devices provide another platform for studying nonequilibrium quantum dynamics [68, 71, 69]. These systems make it possible to investigate QKZM in two- and three-dimensional (3D) settings and to use its scaling predictions as a probe of the quantumness of the hardware [91, 68, 44, 116, 43, 8, 105, 1, 148].

Quantum simulations can be also benchmarked against classical simulation methods, including tensor network (TN) approaches. One of the most prominent examples are matrix product states (MPS) [50, 118]. While MPS are extremely powerful for one-dimensional (1D) systems, their application to 2D is typically limited to relatively small system sizes. This limitation does not apply to projected entangled-pair states (PEPS) [90, 53, 138, 88, 63, 62, 139, 93, 95, 79, 94, 27, 136, 51, 145, 26, 24, 102, 103, 57], which provide a natural generalization of MPS to higher dimensions, including 3D [141, 80].

In Ref. 69, the coherent annealer was benchmarked against classical simulation methods in several QKZM scenarios for the random Ising model, demonstrating an advantage of the quantum device across a range of setups. In particular, for a cubic lattice, the main bottleneck of classical PEPS simulations was identified as the evaluation of expectation values. In this work, we revisit this problem using both deterministic and Monte Carlo approaches. The latter allows us to estimate the final excitation energy of the system across the full range of quench times accessible to classical simulations. This development effectively shifts the computational bottleneck back to the time-evolution simulation itself, which must now be extended to cover a broader range of quench times. Beyond the annealing scenario, the Monte Carlo scheme can also find applications in other problems, such as computing ground state properties [141, 80].

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we briefly outline quantum annealing as implemented in the D-Wave quantum annealer. In Sec. III, we describe the simulation of time evolution using a 3D tensor network. In Sec. IV, expectation values are computed deterministically within the network, while Sec. V presents an alternative approach based on Monte Carlo sampling. Finally, we conclude in Sec. VI.

II Quantum annealing

We consider a 3D transverse-field quantum Ising model on a cubic lattice. In a parametrization suitable for quantum annealing, its Hamiltonian is given by[69]

ℋ⁡(s)\displaystyle{\cal H}(s) =\displaystyle= Γ⁡(s)​ℋD+𝒥⁡(s)​ℋI,\displaystyle\Gamma(s)\;{\cal H}_{D}+{\cal J}(s)\;{\cal H}_{I}, (4)
ℋD\displaystyle{\cal H}_{D} =\displaystyle= −∑iσxi,\displaystyle-\sum_{i}\sigma^{x}_{i}, (5)
ℋI\displaystyle{\cal H}_{I} =\displaystyle= ∑i​jJi​j​σiz​σjz.\displaystyle\sum_{ij}J_{ij}\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}. (6)

Here, σix\sigma^{x}_{i} and σiz\sigma^{z}_{i} denote Pauli operators acting on spin (qubit) ii, and s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1] is a dimensionless time-like parameter, see Fig. 1. In this work, we consider a cubic lattice with only nearest-neighbor (NN) couplings Ji​jJ_{ij}, randomly and uniformly distributed between ±1\pm 1. The transverse field Γ⁡(s)\Gamma(s) and the energy scale of the Ising Hamiltonian 𝒥⁡(s){\cal J}(s) are shown in Fig. 1. The parameter ss is ramped from 00 to 11 over the annealing time tat_{a}, according to s=t/tas=t/t_{a}. During this process, the Hamiltonian evolves from a nearly pure transverse-field Hamiltonian to the pure Ising Hamiltonian.

The evolution begins in the ground state of the initial Hamiltonian. Upon crossing the quantum phase transition from the paramagnetic phase to the spin-glass phase, excitations are generated in accordance with QKZM. The relevant critical exponents are 1/ν=1.551/\nu=1.55 and z=1.3z=1.3 [70]. The residual excitation energy per spin in the Ising Hamiltonian at the end of the ramp is predicted [70] to scale as

Q∝ta−(dν+zν−1)/(1+zν)=ta−0.965,Q\propto t_{a}^{-(d\nu+z\nu-1)/(1+z\nu)}=t_{a}^{-0.965}, (7)

where d=3d=3 is the spatial dimensionality. The power law holds for long enough annealing time provided that the Kibble–Zurek correlation length imprinted on the state after crossing the critical point,

ξ^∝ta0.35,\hat{\xi}\propto t_{a}^{0.35}, (8)

remains small compared with the system size. In the following we attempt to test the energy power law with the 3D PEPS.

III Time evolution

Figure 2(a) shows the PEPS tensor-network ansatz on a cubic lattice. The diagram represents the probability amplitude ψi1​i2​…\psi_{i_{1}i_{2}...} of the state

∑i1​i2​…ψi1​i2​…​|i1​i2​…⟩.\sum_{i_{1}i_{2}...}\psi_{i_{1}i_{2}...}\mbox{$|i_{1}i_{2}...\rangle$}. (9)

The amplitude is obtained by contracting the tensor network:

ψi1​i2​…=Tr​A1i1​A2i2​….\psi_{i_{1}i_{2}...}={\rm Tr~}A^{i_{1}}_{1}A^{i_{2}}_{2}\dots. (10)

Here AjijA^{i_{j}}_{j} is the tensor at site jj with physical index iji_{j}, and Tr denotes contraction of the tensors over their virtual indices, as illustrated in Fig. 2(a). In two dimensions, iPEPS has been used to simulate sudden Hamiltonian quenches [29, 60, 59, 72, 73, 47, 48, 64, 65, 41, 4]. The neighborhood tensor update (NTU) [47], that is employed here, has been applied to simulations of many-body localization [48], Kibble-Zurek ramps [116, 41, 69, 149], the bang-bang preparation of ground states using shallow quantum circuits [150, 128], as well as thermal states obtained by imaginary-time evolution in the fermionic Hubbard model [124, 127, 151].

Unitary time evolution of the 3D PEPS is implemented using nn finite time steps of equal duration d​tdt,

e−i​d​t​ℋ​(s1)​…​e−i​d​t​ℋ​(sn),e^{-idt{\cal H}(s_{1})}\dots e^{-idt{\cal H}(s_{n})}, (11)

where ta=n​d​tt_{a}=n~dt is the total anneal time and sk=(k−1/2)​d​t/tas_{k}=(k-1/2)dt/t_{a}. Within the second-order Suzuki-Trotter decomposition, we approximate

e−i​d​t​ℋ​(sk)≈e−i​d​t2​Γ​(sk)​ℋD​e−i​d​t​𝒥​(sk)​ℋI​e−i​d​t2​Γ​(sk)​ℋD.e^{-idt{\cal H}(s_{k})}\approx e^{-\frac{idt}{2}\Gamma(s_{k}){\cal H}_{D}}e^{-idt{\cal J}(s_{k}){\cal H}_{I}}e^{-\frac{idt}{2}\Gamma(s_{k}){\cal H}_{D}}. (12)

Here the driving term is a product of one-site gates:

e−i​d​t2​Γ​(sk)​ℋD=∏jei​d​t2​Γ​(sk)​σjx.e^{-\frac{idt}{2}\Gamma(s_{k}){\cal H}_{D}}=\prod_{j}e^{\frac{idt}{2}\Gamma(s_{k})\sigma^{x}_{j}}. (13)

Its application to the ansatz in Figure 2(a) is straightforward: the (transpose of each) one-site gate is applied to the corresponding physical index of the tensor network. The interaction term is a product of mutually commuting NN Ising gates:

e−i​d​t​𝒥​(sk)​ℋI=∏⟨i​j⟩e−i​d​t​𝒥​(sk)​Ji​j​σiz​σjz.\displaystyle e^{-idt{\cal J}(s_{k}){\cal H}_{I}}=\prod_{\langle ij\rangle}e^{-idt{\cal J}(s_{k})J_{ij}\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}}. (14)

Each NN Trotter gate can be written as a sum of two terms:

e−i​d​t​𝒥​(sk)​Ji​j​σiz​σjz=1i1jcosϕi​j−iσziσzjsinϕi​j,e^{-idt{\cal J}(s_{k})J_{ij}\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}}=1_{i}1_{j}\cos\phi_{ij}-i\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}\sin\phi_{ij}, (15)

where ϕi​j=d​t​𝒥​(sk)​Ji​j\phi_{ij}=dt{\cal J}(s_{k})J_{ij}. This sum can be expressed in the more compact form

∑m=1,2Tim​Tjm,\sum_{m=1,2}T_{i}^{m}T_{j}^{m}, (16)

where the one-site operators are Ti1=1i​cos⁡ϕi​jT_{i}^{1}=1_{i}\sqrt{\cos\phi_{ij}} and Ti2=σiz​−isinϕi​jT_{i}^{2}=\sigma^{z}_{i}\sqrt{-i\sin\phi_{ij}}. The resulting expression can be viewed as a contraction of two tensors over a common bond index mm of dimension 22. Therefore, an Ising Trotter gate applied to a nearest-neighbor (NN) bond doubles the bond dimension from DD to 2​D2D. To prevent the exponential growth of the bond dimension during time evolution, it must be truncated back to DD. This truncation is performed using the neighborhood tensor update (NTU), for numerical details see Ref. 47.

Figure 3 illustrates two of the tensor neighborhoods used in the NTU truncation [69]. On the one hand, larger neighborhoods provide more accurate truncations, as the resulting Gram-Schmidt metric tensor more faithfully represents the tensor environment, enabling more efficient use of the limited bond dimension. On the other hand, the computational cost of exact tensor contraction increases rapidly with neighborhood size. Unlike in two dimensions [47], in 3D we cannot afford neighborhoods containing closed loops. These loops are approximated using SVD1 truncations. This mean-field-like approximation is expected to provide a better description than neglecting loops altogether, as in the simple-update scheme [94] or its belief-propagation variant [131]. With or without the SVD1 approximations, the resulting metric tensor remains Hermitian and non-negative, ensuring stable bond-dimension truncation. The contraction of both Gram-Schmidt metric tensors presented in Fig. 3 has a computational cost scaling as 𝒪⁡(D8){\cal O}\left(D^{8}\right). In this paper we employ the method in Fig. 3(b).

The time evolution is performed for a range of ramp times for both an infinite lattice with periodic randomness and an L3L^{3} unit cell, and a finite lattice with open boundary conditions (PBC and OBC). The time step is d​t=0.01​nsdt=0.01\mathrm{ns}, which is sufficiently small for the two coefficients shown in Fig. 1, particularly in the regime where their magnitudes are comparable. The residual excitation energy near the end of the ramp - specifically at s=0.6s=0.6, when the transverse field is already negligible - is evaluated using deterministic methods for PBC [141, 80] and Monte Carlo methods for OBC. It is defined as

Q=𝒩−1​∑⟨i​j⟩[⟨σiz​σjz⟩−⟨σiz​σjz⟩GS].Q={\cal N}^{-1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left[\left\langle\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}\right\rangle-\left\langle\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}\right\rangle_{\rm GS}\right]. (17)

Here, the sum runs over all NN bonds-within the unit cell for PBC and over the open lattice for OBC-and 𝒩{\cal N} is the total number of bonds. ⟨…⟩\langle\dots\rangle denotes the expectation value in the quantum state near the end of the ramp, while ⟨…⟩GS\langle\dots\rangle_{\rm GS} denotes the value in the ground state of the classical Hamiltonian ℋI{\cal H}_{I} in Eq. (4). Anticipating the KZ correlation length (8) to remain much shorter than LL even for the longest considered anneal times, the number of disorder samples is one. The results are effectively self-averaged over the disorder within the L×L×LL\times L\times L lattice (or unit cell). The size L=8L=8 is considered.

The tensor network is evolved with a fixed bond dimension DD throughout the dynamics. In the final state, it is occasionally truncated to a smaller bond dimension to facilitate the evaluation of the energy. The final truncation is done in the same way as after a Trotter gate. In Figs. 4 and 8, this is denoted as D=(De,Dt)D=(D_{e},D_{t}), where DeD_{e} is the bond dimension used during the evolution and DtD_{t} is the truncated bond dimension used for the final energy evaluation.

IV Deterministic expectation values

The deterministic evaluation combines the methods of Ref. 141 and Ref. 80, as illustrated in Fig. 4. Panel (a) shows the iPEPS ansatz with a periodic unit cell of size L3L^{3} corresponding to the periodicity of the disorder. In (b), the iPEPS is contracted through the physical indices with its conjugate to form a tensor network representing its norm squared. The zz-th horizontal layer of the norm is treated as a transfer matrix 𝒯z{\cal T}_{z}. The transfer matrices are periodic, 𝒯z±L=𝒯z{\cal T}_{z\pm L}={\cal T}_{z}, and each transfer matrix has a periodic L2L^{2} unit cell. We seek the leading upper and lower eigenvectors, |𝒰z)\left|{\cal U}_{z}\right) and (ℒz|\left({\cal L}_{z}\right|, represented by the iPEPS shown in panels (c) and (i), respectively. For the leading eigenvalue Λ\Lambda, they satisfy

Λ|𝒰z)\displaystyle\Lambda\left|{\cal U}_{z}\right) =\displaystyle= 𝒯z…𝒯z+L−1|𝒰z),\displaystyle{\cal T}_{z}\dots{\cal T}_{z+L-1}\left|{\cal U}_{z}\right), (18)
Λ(ℒz|\displaystyle\Lambda\left({\cal L}_{z}\right| =\displaystyle= (ℒz|𝒯z−L+1…𝒯z.\displaystyle\left({\cal L}_{z}\right|{\cal T}_{z-L+1}\dots{\cal T}_{z}. (19)

These boundary iPEPS have a periodic L2L^{2} unit cell and bond dimension dd. Along the vertical direction, with layers labeled by the index zz, there is a periodic sequence of LL distinct upper and lower boundary states. These boundary states are obtained using the power method suggested by (18) and (19). Each horizontal layer of the double-PEPS network in Fig. 2(b) acts as a transfer matrix that is repeatedly applied to the boundary state until convergence is achieved. Since 𝒯z{\cal T}_{z} is double-layered, its application to 𝒰z+1{\cal U}_{z+1} is carried out in two steps, as shown in Fig. 2(d,f,g,h). First, only the zz-th iPEPS layer is applied, as shown in Fig. 2(d). After this application, the boundary bond dimension is truncated back to dd in Fig. 2(f) to prevent uncontrolled growth. The resulting truncated iPEPS is a mixed upper boundary, |Uz)\left|U_{z}\right), with additional physical indices. Next, the zz-th conjugate iPEPS layer is applied, as shown in Fig. 2(g). After a second truncation, it becomes the upper boundary |𝒰z)\left|{\cal U}_{z}\right) shown in Fig. 2(h).

The truncations are performed using the simple-update (SU) scheme, as illustrated in Fig. 2(e). For numerical details, see Ref. [92] for a general discussion and Refs. [141, 80] for the present context. To perform the SVD efficiently, the left and right halves of the diagram are first decomposed using QR factorization, yielding reduced matrices whose product is then subjected to an SVD. The computational cost of the QR decomposition is 𝒪⁡(D7​d5​p){\cal O}\left(D^{7}d^{5}p\right), where p=2p=2 is the physical dimension.

After all LL upper and lower boundaries have converged, the corresponding mixed boundaries are contracted together as (Lz|Uz)\left(L_{z}\right|\left.U_{z}\right), see Fig. 2(j). The result is a two-dimensional tensor network with an L×LL\times L unit cell. It is approximately contracted using the corner transfer matrix renormalization group (CTMRG) [93, 25, 27] method with bond dimension χ\chi. The CTMRG procedure for a periodic network with an L2L^{2} unit cell is described in the Appendix of Ref. 25. The leading computational cost of CTMRG arises from singular-value decompositions of enlarged corner tensors and scales as 𝒪⁡(d6​χ3){\cal O}\left(d^{6}\chi^{3}\right).

The residual energy as a function of the annealing time is shown in Fig. 2 on a log-log scale. For annealing times approaching 3​ns3\mathrm{ns}, the data begin to approach the slope predicted by the Kibble-Zurek power law (7), which is expected to hold for sufficiently long annealing times, provided that the KZ correlation length (8) remains much smaller than LL.

The evaluation of the upper and lower boundary states constitutes the primary computational bottleneck of the method, as it relies on large singular value decompositions. In the present calculations, the largest bond dimension d=7d=7 was chosen such that the truncation error - defined as the sum of discarded singular values divided by the sum of all singular values in Fig. 2(e) - remains below 0.010.01, even for the slowest annealing ramps. For each pair D,dD,d, the energy is converged with respect to the CTMRG bond dimension χ\chi.

V Monte Carlo sampling

We adapt the Monte Carlo (MC) Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to evaluate expectation values on a finite L3=83L^{3}=8^{3} lattice with open boundary conditions. Its main advantage is that, instead of using the full PEPS shown in Fig. 2(a), the algorithm operates on a projected PEPS in which the physical indices are fixed, as illustrated in Fig. 5(a). This eliminates the need for a double-layer network, such as the one shown in Fig. 2(b).

The projected PEPS in Fig. 5(a) represents the probability amplitude for a given configuration of physical indices. Each horizontal layer can be regarded as a transfer matrix 𝒯z{\cal T}_{z}, with z=1,…,Lz=1,\ldots,L. To treat all layers on an equal footing, we assume that, in the special case of z=1z=1, 𝒯1{\cal T}_{1} has upper indices of dimension DD but is nonzero only when these upper indices take the value 11. Similarly, 𝒯L{\cal T}_{L} has lower indices of dimension DD. We can then define upper and lower PEPS boundary states, |𝒰z)\left|{\cal U}_{z}\right) and (ℒz|\left({\cal L}_{z}\right|, for z=0,…,L+1z=0,\ldots,L+1. Each is represented by an L×LL\times L PEPS with bond dimension dd and “physical” dimension DD. The states |𝒰0)\left|{\cal U}_{0}\right) and (ℒL+1|\left({\cal L}_{L+1}\right| are trivial, i.e., their tensors are nonzero only when all bond indices and the physical index are equal to 11. Starting from the trivial |𝒰0)\left|{\cal U}_{0}\right) (or (ℒL+1|\left({\cal L}_{L+1}\right|), the upper (lower) boundary states are obtained by successive application of the transfer matrices, with each application followed by SU truncation of the bond indices:

|𝒰z)\displaystyle\left|{\cal U}_{z}\right) ≈SU\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm SU}}{{\approx}} 𝒯z|𝒰z−1),\displaystyle{\cal T}_{z}\left|{\cal U}_{z-1}\right), (20)
(ℒz|\displaystyle\left({\cal L}_{z}\right| ≈SU\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm SU}}{{\approx}} (ℒz+1|𝒯z.\displaystyle\left({\cal L}_{z+1}\right|{\cal T}_{z}. (21)

Importantly, the bond dimension dd of these boundary states—whose computation remains the main computational bottleneck—can be chosen to be smaller than that required for the double-layer network shown in Fig. 2(c). With the upper and lower boundaries at hand, the probability amplitude in Fig. 5(a) can be evaluated as

(ℒz+1|𝒯z|𝒰z−1),\left({\cal L}_{z+1}\right|{\cal T}_{z}\left|{\cal U}_{z-1}\right), (22)

i.e., by sandwiching a layer of the projected PEPS between the corresponding upper and lower boundaries, as shown in Fig. 5(b). The SU updates in Eqs. (20) and (21) are performed in a manner similar to that shown in Fig. 2(c–h), although there is no need to introduce mixed boundaries. The computational cost of the QR decomposition in the simple update is 𝒪⁡(D6​d5){\cal O}\left(D^{6}d^{5}\right), i.e., formally lower by a factor of D​pDp than in the double-layer deterministic method. Furthermore, the smaller required bond dimension dd yields an additional reduction in the computational cost.

The trade-off is the need for sampling to estimate observables. Here, we sample in the computational σz\sigma^{z} eigenbasis, though other bases can be accessed via a suitable unitary transformation of the physical indices. Sampling proceeds by updating pairs of physical indices. Fig. 5(b) shows a triple-layer network representing amplitudes for different combinations of a chosen pair of indices. This triple-layer network is converted into a planar network (Fig. 6(a)) by defining planar tensors as in Fig. 5(c).

The L×LL\times L planar network is approximately contracted by updating its upper and lower matrix product state (MPS) boundaries, as outlined in Figs. 6(d–f), using the zipper method described in detail in Ref. [126]. Each row xx of the planar network in Fig. 6(a) is treated as a transfer matrix 𝒯x{\cal T}_{x}. The transfer matrices are repeatedly applied to the upper and lower boundaries, |𝒰x)\left|{\cal U}_{x}\right) and (ℒx|\left({\cal L}_{x}\right|, with x=0,…,L+1x=0,\dots,L+1. An upper boundary is shown in Fig. 6(b). It is an MPS in right-canonical form, with isometries satisfying the right-canonical gauge condition shown in Fig. 6(c). For an introduction to matrix product states, see the review in Ref. [137]. In general, each new boundary is obtained from the previous one by applying the transfer matrix, followed by a truncation of the bond dimension:

𝒯x|𝒰x−1)≈zip.|𝒰x),(ℒx+1|𝒯x≈zip.(ℒx|.\displaystyle{\cal T}_{x}\left|{\cal U}_{x-1}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm zip.}}{{\approx}}\left|{\cal U}_{x}\right),~~~~\left({\cal L}_{x+1}\right|{\cal T}_{x}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm zip.}}{{\approx}}\left({\cal L}_{x}\right|. (23)

However, in the zipper method the matrix product operator (MPO) 𝒯x{\cal T}_{x} is not applied in its entirety and truncated only afterward, bond by bond. Instead, during a left-to-right sweep, one MPO tensor is applied at a time, as shown in Fig. 6(e), followed immediately by SVD truncation. The SVD constitutes the leading computational cost of the zipper method, scaling as 𝒪⁡(D3​d6​χ3){\cal O}\left(D^{3}d^{6}\chi^{3}\right). A by-product of this procedure is the mixed boundary obtained halfway through each transfer-matrix application, as shown in Fig. 6(d,f). These mixed boundaries are in the mixed-canonical form, with the tensors to the right (left) of the orthogonality center (OC) in the right- (left-) canonical form. By repeatedly applying the transfer matrix to the upper and lower boundaries, one obtains LL upper and lower boundaries together with the corresponding intermediate mixed boundaries. The upper and lower mixed boundaries can then be combined to evaluate probability amplitudes for different spin configurations. Figure 6(g) shows the diagram for a two-spin probability amplitude Ak​lA_{kl}, assuming that all other spins are fixed. Its value is obtained by shifting the upper orthogonality center (OC) in Fig. 6(g) two sites to the right and then contracting the upper and lower boundaries, as shown in Fig. 6(h). This amplitude is then used to update the two spins.

As in the Metropolis-Hastings MC algorithm, new values of the indices (k,l)(k,l) are proposed according to a simple proposal function based on the local probability ∝Pk​l\propto P_{kl} (Fig. 7). The target probability, ∝|Ak​l|2\propto|A_{kl}|^{2}, then determines whether the proposed indices are accepted. We do not employ the more accurate proposal functions considered in 2D [140], as their evaluation incurs substantial computational overhead, while even this simplest proposal function already yields short autocorrelation times.

The residual energy as a function of the annealing time is shown in Fig. 8 on a log-log scale. For annealing times around 55ns, the data approach the slope predicted by the Kibble-Zurek power law (7). This residual energy decreases for longer annealing times and therefore requires more extensive sampling to achieve the same relative accuracy. The MC sweeps are performed layer by layer and, within each layer, row by row. There are three possible layer orientations and, for each of them, two row orientations. Equivalently, there are six different ways to sweep the 3D lattice, which are applied sequentially. The number of MC sweeps increases from 16×616\times 6 for the fastest ramps to 420×6420\times 6 for the slowest ones in order to maintain the same relative error estimate δ​Q/Q=0.01\delta Q/Q=0.01. The autocorrelation time is on the order of a few sweeps. To estimate the error bars, the data are averaged over blocks of 6 sweeps, and the statistical error is then calculated from these block averages.

Having accumulated all the MC samples, it is straightforward to estimate the correlation function

CR=𝒩R−1​∑⟨i,j⟩R|⟨σiz​σjz⟩|.C_{R}={\cal N}^{-1}_{R}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle_{R}}\left|\langle\sigma^{z}_{i}\sigma^{z}_{j}\rangle\right|. (24)

Here, the sum runs over all pairs of sites i,ji,j separated by a distance RR along x,yx,y or zz direction, and 𝒩R{\cal N}_{R} is the number of such pairs. Fig. 9 shows the correlator obtained from the MC-estimated expectation values. According to the KZ mechanism, its range should increase as (8). The correlators for ta=2.56,5.12t_{a}=2.56,5.12ns are not inconsistent with this prediction. Importantly, for self-consistency, these correlators are still short-ranged when compared to the size of the lattice.

Finally, in Fig. 10, we compare the most accurate results from Figs. 4 and 8. Although there is a slight systematic difference between the infinite lattice with periodic disorder and the open lattice, both datasets exhibit the same dependence. For the deterministic evaluation, the missing 5.12​ns5.12\mathrm{ns} data point proved to be particularly time-consuming because its long correlations led to slow convergence of the computationally expensive upper and lower boundaries. In contrast, the Monte Carlo data extend into the Kibble-Zurek scaling regime.

VI Conclusion

In Ref. [69], the estimation of expectation values in the 3D tensor network was identified as the main bottleneck in tensor-network simulations of quantum annealing. In this work, we show that observables can be evaluated either using deterministic methods or, more efficiently, via 3D Monte Carlo sampling. The sampling over an open-boundary network proceeds layer by layer and, within each layer, row by row, employing 2D PEPS and 1D MPS boundaries, respectively. As a result, the computational bottleneck shifts to the simulation of the time evolution. This bottleneck is less restrictive in the case of imaginary-time evolution toward the ground state [141, 80], which is where the Monte Carlo approach can be particularly advantageous.

The advantage of the Monte Carlo approach stems from the single-layer structure of the involved tensor networks, which drastically reduces the contraction cost compared to the double-layer networks required in deterministic evaluations. In the application considered here, the computational gain from the single-layer structure outweighs the cost of multiple Monte Carlo sweeps required to achieve the desired error bars.

The data used for Figs. 4 and 8 are openly available from https://doi.org/10.57903/UJ/XQWNGX.
